idiom_name: filter() over any callable criterion (functions, lambdas, __call__ objects, functools.partial) + comprehension form
implementation_notes: Any callable is a criterion: filter(function, iterable) builds a lazy iterator of the elements for which the function is true and is documented as equivalent to the predicate form of a generator expression, while comprehensions are the idiomatic spelling when the criterion is a simple expression. Parameterised criteria stay first-class through closures, functools.partial or predicate objects (instances defining __call__), and itertools.filterfalse provides the negation. What replaces the classic filterer structure is the container's own two-line method - def filtered(self, predicate): return replace(self, threats=tuple(t for t in self.threats if predicate(t))) - with dataclasses.replace/type(self) preserving the container's identity and subtype. A hand-written Filterer class is justified only when criteria must be introspectable data (names, negation, serialisable parameters); that is the Specification pattern rather than this one.
pitfalls: filter() returns an iterator that is exhausted after one pass (and filter(None, it) selects by truthiness, not by a criterion), so a 'filtered container' built from it must be materialised.
Late-binding closures capture the variable, not its value: a lambda created in a loop sees the last value, so bind the parameter (lambda t, threshold=threshold: ...) or use functools.partial.
Predicates that mutate the container they are iterating (or that call code which does) raise on dict/set mutation or corrupt the result; criteria must be pure readers.
filter over a mapping yields keys only - filtering a dict by value requires items() and rebuilding, which is easy to forget.
